title: Token Cliffs and Unlock Pressure
objectives: Model what a cliff unlock actually sends into the market
Judge whether the pool is deep enough to absorb it
Tell a stream and a cliff apart when the total unlocked is identical
Watch an unlock happen yourself on a block explorer

steps.title: The Anatomy of an Unlock Event
steps.body:
Locked supply is water held behind a dam. For months the reservoir just sits there. Then the first <Term id="cliff">cliff</Term> opens its gates and a wall of supply rushes the market all at once. That is an unlock event.

What actually happens at the milestone:

- The project reaches its first major cliff — often month 12 — and thousands of early investors and team members suddenly hold transferable tokens.
- Founders who believe in the project may keep holding. Venture funds usually cannot: they are legally bound to return capital to their limited partners.
- As a result a large share — commonly 20% to 60% — of the newly <Term id="unlock">unlocked</Term> tokens goes straight to DEXs to be sold for USDC or SOL.
- The <Term id="liquidity_pool">liquidity pool</Term> on the other side of that trade absorbs every sell order, and its shape decides the damage.

Two framings to carry forward:

- An unlock does not guarantee a crash. It creates structural sell pressure that demand has to outweigh.
- Your job is not to predict the price. It is to measure the pressure against the pool's ability to absorb it.

steps.title: Why AMM Pool Depth Dictates Survival
steps.body:
Drop a boulder into a bathtub and the water goes over the sides. Drop the same boulder into a swimming pool and it barely ripples. Sell pressure works the same way against <Term id="amm">AMM</Term> liquidity: the size of the pool, not the size of the headline, decides the splash.

Recall the constant product formula `x · y = k`.

- When a large dump of tokens enters a <Term id="liquidity_pool">pool</Term>, the spot price moves with the order relative to reserves.
- The bigger the sell against the reserves already inside, the more violent the <Term id="price_impact">price impact</Term> and <Term id="slippage">slippage</Term>.

Compare two pools absorbing the same unlock:

- **Shallow pool:** $1M of reserves. Dumping $2M of unlocked tokens causes catastrophic slippage, crashing the token by 60% or more.
- **Deep pool:** $20M+ spread across Orca and Raydium. The same sell flow is swallowed with only minor price degradation.

This is why careful analysts always compare the upcoming monthly unlock size directly against daily DEX liquidity before forming any view.

steps.title: Cliff Shock vs. Smooth Linear Streaming
steps.body:
Two projects can release the exact same number of tokens and produce completely different price behaviour. The difference is not *how much* unlocks — it is *when*, and how evenly it spreads.

The two dominant designs:

- **Lump-sum monthly cliffs.** A giant bucket drops on the first of each month. This creates predictable dump dates that short sellers can front-run, amplifying downward <Term id="slippage">slippage</Term>.
- **Streaming linear <Term id="vesting">vesting</Term>.** Services like Streamflow unlock tokens smoothly every second, so supply is diffused continuously instead of bursting.

Why streaming usually holds up better:

- Continuous flow lets regular protocol revenue and retail demand absorb the float organically.
- There is no single dramatic date for bots to cluster around, so the front-runnable event largely disappears.
- A <Term id="cliff">cliff</Term> concentrates pressure into one moment, which makes unlock shock as much a timing problem as a volume problem.

steps.title: Under the Hood: How MEV Bots Front-Run Unlocks
steps.body:
On Solana transactions are public before they finalise, so an unlock is never a surprise to the bots watching for it. Searchers behave like hawks circling a feeding schedule they already know by heart.

The front-running playbook:

- Searcher bots monitor the vesting escrow contract addresses directly.
- The instant the <Term id="unlock">unlock</Term> transaction confirms on-chain, they anticipate the incoming DEX sell flow.
- They may short the token on perps, or pull <Term id="liquidity_pool">pool</Term> liquidity to widen the bid-ask spread and profit from the resulting <Term id="slippage">slippage</Term>.
- Because that value is extracted from ordinary traders, it is a form of MEV built on <Term id="amm">AMM</Term> mechanics.

How a careful analyst tracks it:

- Follow the vesting contract balance on Solscan to see exactly when tokens are claimed.
- Watch for those tokens moving into exchange deposit accounts — that is the tell that supply is about to hit the market.
- Reading the chain before the crowd is how you turn a chaotic unlock into a measured, evidence-based view.

questions.prompt: An upcoming unlock will release $10M of tokens, but the token's AMM pool holds only $2M of liquidity. If recipients sell, what is the most likely outcome?
options: The AMM will reject the sell orders because they exceed the pool reserves
The pool will automatically mint new USDC to absorb the sells
Severe price impact and slippage will drive the token price down sharply
Validators will burn the surplus tokens to protect the peg
questions.explainRight: In a constant-product AMM the price moves continuously as reserves shift, so a sell far larger than the pool drives the price down hard. There is no order book to absorb it — the pool itself is the only buyer.
questions.explainWrong: AMMs never reject trades or mint free liquidity; they simply reprice along the x · y = k curve. A $10M sell against a $2M pool overwhelms the reserves.

questions.prompt: Why is continuous per-second streaming vesting generally healthier for a token's price than large monthly cliff unlocks?
options: It removes all transaction fees from the liquidity pool
It permanently locks tokens for at least 100 years
It blocks the token from ever being traded on aggregators
It prevents large, predictable dump events that traders can front-run
questions.explainRight: Streaming diffuses supply in tiny amounts around the clock, so demand absorbs it gradually instead of in one frightening hit. It also removes the obvious date on which short sellers and bots pile in.
questions.explainWrong: Streaming does not change fees or lockups — it changes the shape of the release. By spreading supply evenly it eliminates the big, front-runnable dump dates that create the worst volatility.

questions.prompt: A trader's swap is quoted at one price but executes at a noticeably worse price. Which pair of terms best describes this?
options: Market Cap and FDV
Price impact (the shift their own order causes) and slippage (the gap between quote and execution)
Cliff and vesting
TVL and APR
questions.explainRight: Price impact is how much the order itself moves the pool; slippage is the gap between the quoted price and the fill. Large orders into shallow pools produce both, and they hit hardest during unlock dumps.
questions.explainWrong: Market cap, FDV, cliffs, and vesting describe token economics, not trade execution. The correct pairing is the order's own market impact plus the quote-to-fill gap.

questions.prompt: On Solana, why can MEV bots react to an unlock event faster than ordinary traders?
options: Transaction and contract data are public, so bots monitoring the escrow can act the moment tokens move
The team privately tells bots the unlock date in advance
Solana validators execute only bot transactions
Unlocks can only be triggered by bots by protocol design
questions.explainRight: On-chain data is transparent, so searcher bots watch vesting escrow addresses continuously and can trade the moment claimed tokens head toward exchanges. Their edge is automation plus public information, not insider tips.
questions.explainWrong: Nobody is feeding bots secret unlock dates. Bots win because they monitor escrow contracts around the clock and react instantly, far faster than a human reading a dashboard.

questions.prompt: A simulator estimates that an upcoming unlock adds 8% to a token's circulating supply. What is the correct way to interpret that output?
options: The token price will fall exactly 8% on the unlock date
It guarantees the price will rise 8% because new supply attracts buyers
It is irrelevant because unlocks never affect price
It models the structural supply pressure the market must absorb, not a precise price forecast
questions.explainRight: Unlock models quantify mechanical supply pressure, but real prices also depend on demand, sentiment, and off-market deals. Treat the output as one input into your reasoning, never as a prophecy.
questions.explainWrong: A supply model is not a price oracle. It measures how much new supply must be absorbed, but demand, sentiment, and OTC trading can change the outcome entirely.

questions.prompt: Two tokens each unlock 10% of circulating supply next month. Token X streams it continuously; Token Y releases it all on a single day. All else equal, which reading is best reasoned?
options: Token Y is safer because clustering supply creates support
Both will behave identically because the total released is the same
Token X likely sees smoother price behavior, while Token Y faces a concentrated, front-runnable sell shock
Token Y likely pumps, because large unlocks attract new buyers
questions.explainRight: Same total supply, very different timing. Streaming lets the market digest supply continuously, while a one-day cliff creates a single moment of maximum pressure that traders can anticipate and front-run.
questions.explainWrong: Equal totals do not mean equal impact, because timing determines how much the pool must absorb at once. A single-day release concentrates all the pressure into one front-runnable moment.

questions.prompt: A token has a $5M liquidity pool. Next month unlocks $5M worth, and the month after unlocks another $5M, with no new demand. What is the most accurate description of the risk?
options: The first unlock can roughly halve the price, and the second hits an even smaller pool, so damage compounds rather than averages out
There is no risk, because each unlock is only equal to the pool's size once
Price impact is linear, so two $5M unlocks cause exactly the same damage as one $10M unlock
A $5M unlock into a $5M pool is trivially absorbed with under 1% impact
questions.explainRight: Once the first dump shrinks the pool and the price, the second unlock is even larger relative to the now-smaller reserves, so each round can hurt more than the last. Unlock pressure compounds when demand does not refill the pool.
questions.explainWrong: Price impact is not linear — it grows as reserves shrink. After the first large dump drains the pool, the second unlock faces thinner liquidity, so the damage compounds instead of averaging out.
